themeName: Theme 1: Introduction to Markets and Market Failure

topics.title: Specialisation and the Division of Labour
Price, Income and Cross Elasticities of Demand

cards.front: What does ceteris paribus mean, and why do economists rely on it?
cards.back:
Ceteris paribus — a Latin phrase meaning ‘all other things being equal’ or ‘all other factors held constant’.

Economists cannot run laboratory experiments, so they isolate the effect of one variable by assuming all others stay constant.

cards.front: Why is economics a social science, and why do economists build models?
cards.back: Economics studies human behaviour, so unlike natural sciences it cannot run controlled laboratory experiments. Economists instead build models — deliberate simplifications of reality — and test them against evidence, holding other factors constant (ceteris paribus) to isolate one relationship at a time.

cards.front: Define a positive statement.
cards.back:
A positive statement is an objective statement about what is, was or will be, which can be tested against evidence and shown to be true or false.

Example: ‘A rise in the minimum wage will increase unemployment’ — testable, whether or not it turns out to be true.

cards.front: Define a normative statement.
cards.back:
A normative statement is a subjective statement of opinion about what ought to be, resting on a value judgement, so it cannot be proved true or false.

Watch for the signal words in exam extracts: should, ought, fair, too much.

cards.front: Define a value judgement.
cards.back:
Value judgement — a view about what is morally or subjectively important. These judgements underpin all normative statements.

Exam link: economic policy always rests on value judgements about whose welfare matters most.

cards.front: Define scarcity — the basic economic problem.
cards.back:
Scarcity — when there are finite resources (e.g., land, labour, capital) but infinite human wants and needs.

Scarcity forces every economic agent to make choices, and every choice carries an opportunity cost.

cards.front: Define opportunity cost.
cards.back:
Opportunity cost — the value of the next best alternative foregone when making an economic decision.

It is the next best alternative that counts, not everything given up.

cards.front: Name and define the four factors of production.
cards.back:
The factors of production are the resources used to produce goods and services:

  • Land — all natural resources.
  • Labour — the human workforce.
  • Capital — man-made aids to production, such as machinery and factories.
  • Enterprise — the entrepreneurship that organises the other factors and bears the risk.

cards.front: Distinguish renewable from non-renewable resources.
cards.back:
Renewable resources can be replenished over time (wind power, solar energy, forests), so their use can be sustainable.

Non-renewable resources — finite and cannot be replenished once depleted (e.g., oil, coal, natural gas). Their use involves a high opportunity cost for future generations.

cards.front: Define a production possibility frontier (PPF).
cards.back:
A production possibility frontier shows the maximum combinations of two goods or services an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed.

Points inside the frontier mean unemployed or inefficiently used resources; points beyond it are currently unattainable.

cards.front: Sketch a PPF and mark an efficient point, an inefficient point and an unattainable point. Where is opportunity cost shown?
cards.back: Points on the frontier (A, C, D, B) are productively efficient — all resources are fully employed. E, inside the frontier, is inefficient; F, outside it, is currently unattainable. Moving from C to D gains consumer goods at the opportunity cost of the capital goods given up.
cards.svgAlt: Concave production possibility frontier for capital and consumer goods with efficient points A, C, D and B on the curve, inefficient point E inside it and unattainable point F outside it

cards.front: Show economic growth and economic decline on a PPF, and give a cause of each.
cards.back:
An outward shift from PPF1 to PPF2 shows economic growth — the economy can produce more of both goods. Causes: investment in capital, technological advance, a larger or better-educated workforce, discovery of resources.

An inward shift from PPF1 to PPF3 shows decline — natural disaster, war, or resource depletion.
cards.svgAlt: Three concentric production possibility frontiers with an outward shift from PPF1 to PPF2 showing growth and an inward shift from PPF1 to PPF3 showing decline

cards.front: Define specialisation.
cards.back: Specialisation — occurs when individuals, firms, regions, or countries concentrate on producing a specific good or service.

cards.front: Define the division of labour.
cards.back:
Division of labour — a form of specialisation where the production process is split into separate tasks, with each worker assigned a specific, repetitive task - this enables the worker to become highly skilled and efficient at that task.

Associated with Adam Smith’s pin factory.

cards.front: Evaluate the division of labour. Give advantages and disadvantages.
cards.back:
• For — workers become highly skilled at one task, raising productivity; time is saved switching between tasks; workers can be matched to their strengths; supports use of specialist machinery.
  • Against — repetitive work breeds boredom and lower motivation; workers' skills narrow, raising the risk of structural unemployment; over-dependence on each stage makes production vulnerable to disruption.

cards.front: Define a free market economy.
cards.back:
A free market economy is one in which resources are allocated by the price mechanism, with supply and demand determining what is produced, how, and for whom — with minimal government intervention.

Associated with Adam Smith’s ‘invisible hand’ and with Hayek; no pure free market exists in practice.

cards.front: Define a command economy.
cards.back:
A command economy is one in which the state owns the means of production and allocates resources through central planning, deciding what is produced and at what price.

Associated with Karl Marx; in practice it suffers information and incentive problems.

cards.front: Define a mixed economy.
cards.back:
A mixed economy combines market allocation with government intervention: most resources are allocated by the price mechanism, while the state provides public goods, corrects market failures and redistributes income.

Every real economy is mixed — economies differ only in where they sit on the spectrum.

cards.front: Evaluate: free market versus command economy. Give the key points each way.
cards.back:
• Free market — prices allocate resources efficiently without a planner; competition drives innovation and choice. But: inequality, externalities ignored, public goods unprovided.
  • Command — can direct resources to social priorities and limit inequality. But: information and incentive problems, shortages and surpluses, little innovation.
  • In practice the debate is about the mix — where intervention improves on the market and where it fails.

cards.front: What does it mean to assume economic agents are rational?
cards.back:
Traditional economic theory assumes agents act rationally — each aims to maximise their own objective: consumers maximise utility, firms maximise profit, and governments maximise social welfare.

Theme 1 also asks you to challenge this assumption — see 1.2.10 on alternative views of consumer behaviour.

cards.front: Define demand.
cards.back:
Demand — the quantity of a good/service consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price in a given time period.

Willing and able — desire without purchasing power is not demand.

cards.front: Sketch the effect of an increase in demand on the demand curve, marking the quantities at the original price.
cards.back: D1 shifts right to D2, caused by a change in a non-price factor — incomes, the price of substitutes or complements, tastes, or population. At the unchanged price P1, quantity demanded rises from Q1 to Q2.
cards.svgAlt: Demand curve D1 shifting right to D2, with quantity demanded rising from Q1 to Q2 at the unchanged price P1

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does a rise in consumer incomes affect the market for a normal good?
cards.back:
Incomes rise, so consumers’ purchasing power rises. At every price they are now willing and able to buy more, shifting demand right from D1 to D2. At the original price there is briefly excess demand, which bids the price up until the market reaches a new equilibrium at a higher price and quantity.

For an inferior good the chain runs the other way — higher incomes shift demand left.

cards.front: State the law of demand.
cards.back: The law of demand — there is an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded (QD). As price rises, QD falls (ceteris paribus).

cards.front: Define marginal utility, and explain how diminishing marginal utility underpins the demand curve.
cards.back:
Marginal utility (MU) — the extra satisfaction from consuming one more unit.

Each additional unit typically adds less satisfaction than the last. Because extra units are worth less to the consumer, they will only buy more at lower prices — which is why the demand curve slopes downwards.

cards.front: List the main conditions of demand — the non-price factors that shift the demand curve.
cards.back:
• Incomes — more for normal goods, less for inferior goods.
  • Prices of related goods — substitutes and complements.
  • Tastes and fashions, including advertising.
  • Population size and structure.
  • Expectations of future prices.

Any of these shifts the whole curve; a change in the good's own price only moves along it.

cards.front: Define price elasticity of demand (PED).
cards.back: PED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in the good's own price.

cards.front: State the formula for price elasticity of demand.
cards.back: Because demand curves slope downwards, PED is negative — interpret its absolute size: elastic if greater than 1, inelastic if less than 1.
cards.formulaHtml: PED=%ΔQD%ΔP\text{PED} = \frac{\%\Delta \text{QD}}{\%\Delta \text{P}}PED=%ΔP%ΔQD​

cards.front: The price of a good rises from £8.00 to £10.00 and quantity demanded falls from 200 to 150 units. Calculate the PED.
cards.back:
%Δ QD = −50 ÷ 200 × 100 = −25%

%Δ P = +£2 ÷ £8 × 100 = +25%

PED = −25% ÷ +25% = −1.0

The percentage fall in quantity exactly matches the percentage rise in price — demand is unit elastic over this price range.

cards.front: Define income elasticity of demand (YED).
cards.back: YED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in consumer income.

cards.front: State the formula for income elasticity of demand, and what its sign tells you.
cards.back: The sign classifies the good: positive for a normal good, negative for an inferior good — and a YED greater than 1 marks a luxury.
cards.formulaHtml: YED=%ΔQD%ΔY\text{YED} = \frac{\%\Delta \text{QD}}{\%\Delta \text{Y}}YED=%ΔY%ΔQD​

cards.front: Define cross elasticity of demand (XED).
cards.back: XED measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded for Good A to a change in the price of Good B.

cards.front: State the formula for cross elasticity of demand, and what its sign tells you.
cards.back: The sign reveals the relationship: positive for substitutes (a dearer rival raises demand for A), negative for complements, and near zero for unrelated goods.
cards.formulaHtml: XED=%ΔQDA%ΔPB\text{XED} = \frac{\%\Delta \text{QD}_{A}}{\%\Delta \text{P}_{B}}XED=%ΔPB​%ΔQDA​​

cards.front: Give the PED value ranges and what each means.
cards.back:
• 0 — perfectly inelastic: quantity does not respond at all.
  • 0 to −1 — price inelastic: quantity changes proportionally less than price.
  • −1 — unit elastic: proportional changes are equal.
  • −1 to −∞ — price elastic: quantity changes proportionally more than price.
  • −∞ — perfectly elastic: any price rise loses all demand.

cards.front: What determines whether a good's demand is price elastic or inelastic?
cards.back:
• Availability of substitutes — the strongest factor: close substitutes make demand elastic.
  • Proportion of income spent on the good — big-ticket items are more elastic.
  • Necessity or luxury — necessities are inelastic.
  • Addictiveness — habit-forming goods are inelastic.
  • Time period — demand becomes more elastic over time as consumers find alternatives.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: a firm sells a good with price inelastic demand. What happens to its total revenue if it raises the price?
cards.back:
Because demand is price inelastic, the percentage fall in quantity demanded is smaller than the percentage rise in price. The revenue gained on each remaining unit outweighs the revenue lost from the units no longer sold, so total revenue rises.

The reverse holds for elastic demand — cutting the price raises revenue. This is why PED is central to firms' pricing decisions.

cards.front: The price of Good B rises by 10%, and the quantity demanded of Good A rises by 5%. Calculate the XED and state the relationship between the goods.
cards.back:
XED = %Δ QD of A ÷ %Δ P of B = +5% ÷ +10% = +0.5

The positive sign means the goods are substitutes; at 0.5 they are fairly weak ones — consumers switch, but not aggressively.

cards.front: Define supply.
cards.back: Supply — the quantity of a good/service producers are willing and able to produce/sell at a given price in a given time period.

cards.front: Sketch the effect of an increase in supply on the supply curve, marking the quantities at the original price.
cards.back: S1 shifts right to S2, caused by a non-price factor — a technological advance, lower costs of production, or a subsidy. At the unchanged price P, quantity supplied rises from Q1 to Q2. A shift left from S2 to S1 could be caused by an increase in costs of production.
cards.svgAlt: Supply curve S1 shifting right to S2, with quantity supplied rising from Q1 to Q2 at the unchanged price P

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: why does the supply curve slope upwards?
cards.back: When the price of a good rises, producing it becomes more profitable at the margin. Existing firms are incentivised to expand output, and in time new firms are attracted into the market. Quantity supplied therefore rises with price — an upward-sloping supply curve.

cards.front: List the main conditions of supply — the non-price factors that shift the supply curve.
cards.back:
• Costs of production — wages, raw materials, energy.
  • Technology — advances shift supply right.
  • Indirect taxes and subsidies.
  • Number of sellers in the market.
  • Supply shocks — weather and disease, especially for agricultural goods.

cards.front: Define price elasticity of supply (PES), and state why it differs between the short run and the long run.
cards.back:
PES measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in the good's price.

In the short run at least one factor of production is fixed, so supply is more price inelastic; in the long run all factors are variable, so supply is more price elastic.

cards.front: State the formula for price elasticity of supply.
cards.back: PES is positive, because supply curves slope upwards: elastic if greater than 1, inelastic if less than 1.
cards.formulaHtml: PES=%ΔQS%ΔP\text{PES} = \frac{\%\Delta \text{QS}}{\%\Delta \text{P}}PES=%ΔP%ΔQS​

cards.front: The price of a good rises from £20.00 to £23.00 and quantity supplied rises from 400 to 430 units. Calculate the PES.
cards.back:
%Δ QS = +30 ÷ 400 × 100 = +7.5%

%Δ P = +£3 ÷ £20 × 100 = +15%

PES = +7.5% ÷ +15% = +0.5

Supply is price inelastic here — firms cannot easily expand output in response to the higher price, as is typical in the short run.

cards.front: What determines whether supply is price elastic or inelastic?
cards.back:
• Spare capacity — idle machines and workers make supply elastic.
  • Stocks — goods that can be stored can be released quickly.
  • Factor mobility — how easily labour and capital can be switched into production.
  • Time period — supply is inelastic in the short run and more elastic in the long run, when all factors are variable.

cards.front: Define market equilibrium.
cards.back:
Market equilibrium — the point where market demand equals market supply.

At the equilibrium price there is neither a shortage nor a surplus, so the price has no tendency to change.

cards.front: Sketch a market in equilibrium, labelling the equilibrium price and quantity.
cards.back: Supply and demand intersect at the equilibrium: price P and quantity Q, marked with dashed lines to each axis. At any other price, excess demand or excess supply moves the market back towards this point.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand curves crossing at equilibrium price P and quantity Q, marked with dashed lines to the axes

cards.front: Distinguish excess demand from excess supply.
cards.back:
Excess demand — at a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage.

Excess supply — at a price above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does the market eliminate excess demand?
cards.back: At a price below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. Competing buyers bid the price up. The rising price causes an extension of supply and a contraction of demand, narrowing the shortage, until the market returns to equilibrium where demand once again equals supply.

cards.front: Show excess demand on a supply and demand diagram, and how the market corrects it.
cards.back: At P1, below the equilibrium Pe, quantity demanded Qd exceeds quantity supplied Qs — the bracketed gap is the shortage. Competing buyers bid the price up (the arrows), causing an extension of supply and a contraction of demand until the market returns to Pe and Qe.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with a price below equilibrium, showing excess demand between Qs and Qd and arrows along both curves pointing up towards equilibrium

cards.front: Show excess supply on a supply and demand diagram, and how the market corrects it.
cards.back: At P1, above the equilibrium Pe, quantity supplied Qs exceeds quantity demanded Qd — the bracketed gap is the surplus. Unsold stock pushes the price down (the arrows), causing a contraction of supply and an extension of demand until the market returns to Pe and Qe.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with a price above equilibrium, showing excess supply between Qd and Qs and arrows along both curves pointing down towards equilibrium

cards.front: Name and define the three functions of the price mechanism.
cards.back:
• Rationing — prices allocate scarce resources to those willing and able to pay.
  • Incentive — price changes motivate producers: high prices encourage more supply, low prices less.
  • Signalling — prices convey information about where resources are needed: a rising price signals scarcity and high demand.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: consumer tastes shift towards a good. How does the price mechanism reallocate resources?
cards.back: Demand shifts right, creating excess demand at the old price, so the price rises. The higher price signals scarcity, rations the good to those willing and able to pay, and incentivises producers to expand output. Resources are drawn into this market from less profitable uses — reallocation with no central direction.

cards.front: Evaluate: the price mechanism allocates resources efficiently. What are the key evaluation points?
cards.back:
• For — no central planner is needed; prices aggregate dispersed information and adjust continuously.
  • Externalities — prices reflect private, not social, costs and benefits, so markets over- or under-provide.
  • Public goods — non-excludability means the mechanism fails to provide them at all.
  • Equity — rationing by willingness and ability to pay can price the poorest out of essentials.

cards.front: Define consumer surplus.
cards.back: Consumer surplus — the difference between what a consumer is willing to pay (their valuation) and what they actually pay. It is a measure of consumer welfare/benefit.

cards.front: Define producer surplus.
cards.back: Producer surplus — the difference between the price a producer is willing to accept (their cost of supply) and the price they actually receive. It is a measure of producer welfare/profit.

cards.front: Define community surplus (social surplus).
cards.back: Community surplus is the sum of consumer and producer surplus. It represents the total welfare in the market, and is maximised at the free-market equilibrium.

cards.front: Show consumer surplus and producer surplus on a supply and demand diagram.
cards.back: At equilibrium price P and quantity Q: consumer surplus is the triangle above P and below the demand curve; producer surplus is the triangle below P and above the supply curve. Together they form the community surplus — the market's total welfare.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with the consumer surplus triangle shaded above price P under the demand curve, and the producer surplus triangle shaded below P above the supply curve

cards.front: Draw how the burden of a specific (per-unit) indirect tax is split between consumers and producers.
cards.back:
The tax shifts supply left from S to S+Tax. The market price rises from P1 to P2 — the consumer burden — while producers keep only P3 after remitting the tax, so P1 to P3 is the producer burden. Output falls from Q1 to Q2.

The more price inelastic demand is, the larger the share of the burden consumers bear.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with supply shifted left to S plus tax, showing the consumer burden between P1 and P2 and the producer burden between P3 and P1, up to the new quantity Q2

cards.front: Evaluate: an indirect tax is an effective way to cut consumption of a demerit good. What are the key evaluation points?
cards.back:
• PED is decisive — if demand is price inelastic, as for addictive goods such as cigarettes, quantity falls little and the tax mainly raises revenue.
  • Regressive burden — indirect taxes take a larger share of low incomes.
  • Unintended consequences — black markets and cross-border shopping can grow.
  • Setting the rate — the external cost is hard to measure, so the tax may over- or under-correct.

cards.front: Give a real-world example of an indirect tax used to correct a market failure in the UK.
cards.back:
The UK Soft Drinks Industry Levy (April 2018) charges 18p per litre on drinks with 5–8g of sugar per 100ml, and 24p per litre above 8g.

Application point: manufacturers reformulated to duck the thresholds — the sugar content of taxed drinks fell by over a third — so the levy worked mainly through supply-side reformulation rather than the price mechanism alone.

cards.front: Define a subsidy.
cards.back: A subsidy is a payment from the government to producers, usually per unit of output, that lowers their costs of production and increases supply — typically granted to goods with positive externalities.

cards.front: Draw how the benefit of a per-unit subsidy is split between consumers and producers.
cards.back:
The subsidy shifts supply right from S to S+Subsidy. The market price falls from P1 to P2 — the consumer gain — while producers receive P3, the market price plus the subsidy, so P1 to P3 is the producer gain. Output rises from Q1 to Q2.

As with a tax, elasticities decide the split: the more price inelastic demand is, the more of the subsidy reaches consumers as a lower price.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with supply shifted right to S plus subsidy, showing the consumer gain between P2 and P1 and the producer gain between P1 and P3, up to the new quantity Q2

cards.front: Show the government revenue raised by a specific indirect tax.
cards.back: The tax shifts supply from S to S+Tax and output falls to Q2. Revenue = tax per unit (P2 to P3) × quantity sold (Q2) — the shaded rectangle. Note that revenue is earned only on the Q2 units still traded, which is why taxes on price inelastic goods raise the most.
cards.svgAlt: Indirect tax diagram with the rectangle between P3 and P2 up to quantity Q2 shaded to show government tax revenue

cards.front: Show the incidence of an indirect tax when demand is price inelastic.
cards.back: With a steep (inelastic) demand curve, the price rises most of the way to the full tax: consumers bear the larger burden (P1 to P2) and producers the smaller (P3 to P1). Quantity falls only slightly — which is why governments tax inelastic goods like fuel and cigarettes: consumption barely falls and revenue is high.
cards.svgAlt: Indirect tax diagram with a steep demand curve, showing a large consumer burden, a small producer burden and only a small fall in quantity

cards.front: Show the incidence of an indirect tax when demand is price elastic.
cards.back: With a shallow (elastic) demand curve, producers cannot pass the tax on: the price rises only slightly (P1 to P2), so producers bear the larger burden (P3 to P1) and quantity falls sharply from Q1 to Q2. Taxing elastic goods cuts consumption effectively but raises little revenue.
cards.svgAlt: Indirect tax diagram with a shallow demand curve, showing a small consumer burden, a large producer burden and a large fall in quantity

cards.front: Evaluate: subsidising a good with positive externalities. What are the key evaluation points?
cards.back:
• Opportunity cost — the subsidy is funded by taxpayers; the money has alternative uses.
  • Elasticity matters — with inelastic demand, output barely rises and the subsidy mostly lifts producer revenue.
  • Dependency — firms may come to rely on the subsidy rather than cutting costs.
  • Setting the level — the external benefit is hard to measure, so the subsidy may over- or under-correct.

cards.front: How does behavioural economics challenge the assumption of rational decision making?
cards.back: Behavioural economics challenges this view, arguing that consumers are often irrational and that their choices are systematically influenced by psychological biases and rules of thumb.

cards.front: Give the specification's three reasons why consumers may not behave rationally.
cards.back:
• Influence of other people's behaviour — herd behaviour and social norms shape choices.
  • Habitual behaviour — defaults and routines persist even against a consumer's own interest.
  • Consumer weakness at computation — people struggle to calculate and compare complex prices, deals and probabilities.

cards.front: Define market failure.
cards.back: Market failure — when the free market, through the price mechanism, fails to allocate scarce resources efficiently, leading to a social welfare loss.

cards.front: Name the specification's three types of market failure.
cards.back:
• Externalities — spillover costs or benefits on third parties that the market ignores.
  • Under-provision of public goods — non-excludability means markets fail to supply them.
  • Information gaps — buyers or sellers lack the information for efficient decisions.

cards.front: Draw the welfare loss caused by a negative production externality.
cards.back: Producers face only their private costs, so external costs are ignored and MSC lies above MPC. The market produces at Q1, where MPC = MPB, but the social optimum is Q2, where MSC = MSB. The shaded triangle between the two is the welfare loss from over-production.
cards.svgAlt: Externality diagram with MSC above S equals MPC and D equals MPB equals MSB, showing market output Q1 beyond the social optimum Q2 and a shaded welfare loss triangle

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: why does a free market over-produce a good with negative production externalities?
cards.back: Producers base output decisions only on their private costs. External costs — pollution, congestion — fall on third parties and never enter the firm’s calculation, so MPC understates MSC. The market price is therefore too low and output settles at Q1, beyond the social optimum Q2, creating a welfare loss on every unit in between.

cards.front: Define an externality.
cards.back: Externality — a positive or negative spillover effect that affects a third party not directly involved in the economic transaction. Also known as external costs or external benefits.

cards.front: Define a merit good.
cards.back:
Merit good — a good that generates positive externalities, benefiting society beyond the private benefits received by the consumer.

Examples: education, healthcare, vaccinations. Markets under-provide them.

cards.front: Define a demerit good.
cards.back:
Demerit good — a good that generates negative externalities, imposing costs on society beyond the private costs incurred by the producer.

Examples: cigarettes, alcohol, gambling. Markets over-provide them.

cards.front: State the relationship between private, external and social costs and benefits.
cards.back:
Social cost = private cost + external cost. Private costs fall on the producers in the transaction; external costs spill over onto third parties.

Social benefit = private benefit + external benefit, on the consumption side. Externality diagrams are built from exactly these gaps: MSC above MPC, or MSB above MPB.

cards.front: Draw the welfare loss caused by a positive consumption externality.
cards.back: Consumers count only their private benefits, so MSB lies above D=MPB. The market consumes at Q1, where MPB = MPC, but the social optimum is Q2, where MSB = MSC. The shaded triangle is the welfare loss from under-consumption — the net social benefit forgone on the units between Q1 and Q2.
cards.svgAlt: Externality diagram with MSB above D equals MPB and S equals MPC equals MSC, showing market output Q1 below the social optimum Q2 and a shaded welfare loss triangle

cards.front: Define a public good and its two characteristics.
cards.back:
A public good is both:

  • Non-excludable — it is impossible or extremely costly to prevent non-payers from consuming the good once it is provided.
  • Non-rival — one person's consumption does not reduce the amount available for others.

Examples: street lighting, national defence, flood defences.

cards.front: Explain the free rider problem, and what it does to the market for public goods.
cards.back: Because a public good is non-excludable, people can benefit without paying — they free ride on others' provision. If everyone reasons this way, no one pays, firms cannot charge, and the market fails to provide the good at all: a missing market. This is why public goods are typically state-provided and funded through taxation.

cards.front: Define asymmetric information.
cards.back:
Asymmetric information — a situation where one party in a transaction has more or better information than the other.

The wider category is an information gap: any party lacking the information needed to make an informed decision.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how does asymmetric information cause market failure in the used-car market?
cards.back: Sellers know a car's true condition; buyers do not. Unable to tell good cars from bad, buyers only offer an average price. That price undervalues good cars, so their owners withdraw them from sale, raising the share of bad cars — which pushes offers lower still. Trades that would benefit both sides never happen: a misallocation of resources driven purely by the information gap.

cards.front: Define a maximum price. Where must it be set to have any effect?
cards.back:
A maximum price (price ceiling) is a legal limit above which the price may not rise, set on goods deemed essential — for example rent controls.

It only binds if set below the equilibrium price; above it, the market equilibrium is unaffected.

cards.front: Draw the effect of a maximum price set below the equilibrium price.
cards.back: At Pmax, quantity demanded rises to Qd while quantity supplied falls to Qs — excess demand of Qd minus Qs. Quantity traded falls from Q1 to Qs, and the shortage must be rationed some other way: queues, waiting lists, or black markets.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with a maximum price line below equilibrium, showing quantity supplied Qs below quantity demanded Qd and the resulting shortage

cards.front: Define a minimum price. Where must it be set to have any effect?
cards.back:
A minimum price (price floor) is a legal limit below which the price may not fall — for example minimum unit pricing for alcohol, or a minimum wage in the labour market.

It only binds if set above the equilibrium price; below it, the market equilibrium is unaffected.

cards.front: Draw the effect of a minimum price set above the equilibrium price.
cards.back: At Pmin, quantity supplied rises to Qs while quantity demanded falls to Qd — excess supply of Qs minus Qd. Quantity traded falls from Q1 to Qd, and the surplus persists unless the government buys it up or producers cut output.
cards.svgAlt: Supply and demand diagram with a minimum price line above equilibrium, showing quantity demanded Qd below quantity supplied Qs and the resulting surplus

cards.front: How do tradable pollution permits work?
cards.back:
Tradable pollution permits — the government can set a cap on total emissions and auction permits that firms must purchase to emit pollutants. These can then be traded on a secondary market.

The cap fixes the quantity of pollution; the permit price internalises the external cost and rewards firms that cut emissions cheaply, since they can sell spare permits.

cards.front: Evaluate: a maximum price makes an essential good affordable. What are the key evaluation points?
cards.back:
• Shortage — the ceiling creates excess demand; those who cannot buy at Pmax may be worse off than at the market price.
  • Elasticities matter — the more elastic supply and demand, the larger the shortage.
  • Black markets — unmet demand invites illegal resale above Pmax.
  • Non-price rationing — queues and waiting lists allocate the good by luck or connections rather than need.
  • Long run — depressed prices deter investment in supply (a common critique of rent controls).

cards.front: Give a real-world example of a minimum price operating in a UK market.
cards.back:
The UK National Living Wage — £12.21 an hour for workers aged 21 and over from April 2025 — is a minimum price in the labour market.

Application point: where it binds above the equilibrium wage, theory predicts excess labour supply; in practice UK employment effects have been small, which examiners reward you for weighing against the diagram's prediction.

cards.front: Evaluate: a minimum price on a demerit good. What are the key evaluation points?
cards.back:
• PED is decisive — if demand is inelastic (alcohol for dependent drinkers), consumption falls little.
  • Regressive — the higher price takes a larger share of low incomes.
  • Surplus problem — in goods markets a binding floor leaves unsold output unless the government buys it.
  • Producer support — unlike a tax, the higher price accrues to sellers, not the state: no revenue to fund treatment or offsets.
  • Substitution — consumers may switch to untaxed or illicit alternatives.

cards.front: Evaluate: tradable pollution permits. What are the key evaluation points?
cards.back:
• Quantity certainty — the cap fixes total emissions directly, unlike a tax.
  • Efficiency — firms with the cheapest abatement cut most and sell spare permits, minimising the total cost of reduction.
  • Price volatility — the permit price can swing, weakening investment incentives.
  • Setting the cap — too generous and the price collapses; monitoring and enforcement are costly.
  • Leakage — production may relocate to countries without a scheme.

cards.front: Give a real-world example of tradable pollution permits in use in the UK.
cards.back:
The UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS, launched January 2021 after leaving the EU scheme) caps emissions from energy-intensive industry, electricity generation and domestic aviation, with the cap tightening over time.

Application point: the cap guarantees the quantity of emissions while the permit price does the rationing — the textbook mechanism operating at national scale.

cards.front: Define government failure.
cards.back: Government failure — when government intervention to correct a market failure results in a larger net welfare loss or a less efficient allocation of resources than before the intervention.

cards.front: Give the specification's four causes of government failure.
cards.back:
• Distortion of price signals — intervention (subsidies, price controls) stops prices reflecting scarcity.
  • Unintended consequences — agents respond in ways policymakers did not predict, such as black markets.
  • Excessive administrative costs — running the intervention can outweigh the welfare it recovers.
  • Information gaps — governments, like markets, must decide without full information, so they can set taxes, subsidies or targets at the wrong level.

cards.front: Build the chain of reasoning: how could a well-intentioned subsidy end in government failure?
cards.back: The government cannot observe the true external benefit, so it sets the subsidy by estimate. Set too high, it pulls resources beyond the social optimum and the excess spending carries an opportunity cost elsewhere. Meanwhile the subsidised price distorts the signals other producers rely on, and firms lobby to keep the payment long after any justification has gone. The intervention can end up creating a larger welfare loss than the market failure it targeted — government failure.
